question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(1,-2)$ to $B(0,0)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(2 y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(x\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the endpoint parametrization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(t)&=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\
&=\langle 1,-2\rangle+t\langle -1,2\rangle \\
&=\langle 1 - t,2 t - 2\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x(t)=1 - t$, $y(t)=2 t - 2$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -1,2\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=2\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=2 y$ and $Q(x,y)=x$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(2\right)\cdot \left(2 t - 2\right)\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=4 - 4 t, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(1 - t\right)\cdot \left(2\right) \\
&=2 - 2 t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(6 - 6 t\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- 3 t^{2} + 6 t\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=- 3 t^{2} + 6 t, \\
F(1)&=- 3 \left(1\right)^{2} + 6 \left(1\right) \\
&=3, \\
F(0)&=- 3 \left(0\right)^{2} + 6 \left(0\right) \\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\
&=\left(3\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=3.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(2,0)$ to $B(1,-2)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(2 x^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(2 y^{2}\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the endpoint parametrization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(t)&=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\
&=\langle 2,0\rangle+t\langle -1,-2\rangle \\
&=\langle 2 - t,- 2 t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x(t)=2 - t$, $y(t)=- 2 t$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -1,-2\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=-2\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=2 x^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=2 y^{2}$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(2\right)\cdot \left(2 - t\right)^{2}\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=- 2 t^{2} + 8 t - 8, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(2\right)\cdot \left(- 2 t\right)^{2}\cdot \left(-2\right) \\
&=- 16 t^{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(- 18 t^{2} + 8 t - 8\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- 6 t^{3} + 4 t^{2} - 8 t\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=- 6 t^{3} + 4 t^{2} - 8 t, \\
F(1)&=- 6 \left(1\right)^{3} + 4 \left(1\right)^{2} - 8 \left(1\right) \\
&=-10, \\
F(0)&=- 6 \left(0\right)^{3} + 4 \left(0\right)^{2} - 8 \left(0\right) \\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\
&=\left(-10\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=-10.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(-6,6)$ to $B(-4,4)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Use the parametrization

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=\langle - 2 t - 2,2 t + 2\rangle,
$$

with parameter bounds chosen to match this traversal, to evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(- x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(1\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Match the parameter to the ordered endpoints:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(2)&=\langle -6,6\rangle=A, \\
\mathbf{r}(1)&=\langle -4,4\rangle=B.
\end{aligned}
$$

The traversal therefore takes $t$ from $2$ to $1$. The order of these bounds records the direction.

Here $x(t)=- 2 t - 2$, $y(t)=2 t + 2$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -2,2\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-2\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=2\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=- x y$ and $Q(x,y)=1$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(-1\right)\cdot \left(- 2 t - 2\right)\cdot \left(2 t + 2\right)\cdot \left(-2\right) \\
&=- 8 t^{2} - 16 t - 8, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(2\right) \\
&=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{2}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{2}^{1}\left(- 8 t^{2} - 16 t - 6\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- \frac{8 t^{3}}{3} - 8 t^{2} - 6 t\right]_{2}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=- \frac{8 t^{3}}{3} - 8 t^{2} - 6 t, \\
F(1)&=- \frac{8 \left(1\right)^{3}}{3} - 8 \left(1\right)^{2} - 6 \left(1\right) \\
&=- \frac{50}{3}, \\
F(2)&=- \frac{8 \left(2\right)^{3}}{3} - 8 \left(2\right)^{2} - 6 \left(2\right) \\
&=- \frac{196}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(2) \\
&=\left(- \frac{50}{3}\right)-\left(- \frac{196}{3}\right) \\
&=\frac{146}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The ordered bounds already enforce the stated traversal; no extra sign reversal is needed.

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(2,0)$ to $B(1,-2)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(1\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the endpoint parametrization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(t)&=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\
&=\langle 2,0\rangle+t\langle -1,-2\rangle \\
&=\langle 2 - t,- 2 t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x(t)=2 - t$, $y(t)=- 2 t$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -1,-2\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=-2\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=x y$ and $Q(x,y)=1$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(2 - t\right)\cdot \left(- 2 t\right)\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=- 2 t^{2} + 4 t, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(-2\right) \\
&=-2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(- 2 t^{2} + 4 t - 2\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- \frac{2 t^{3}}{3} + 2 t^{2} - 2 t\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=- \frac{2 t^{3}}{3} + 2 t^{2} - 2 t, \\
F(1)&=- \frac{2 \left(1\right)^{3}}{3} + 2 \left(1\right)^{2} - 2 \left(1\right) \\
&=- \frac{2}{3}, \\
F(0)&=- \frac{2 \left(0\right)^{3}}{3} + 2 \left(0\right)^{2} - 2 \left(0\right) \\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\
&=\left(- \frac{2}{3}\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=- \frac{2}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

$$
\int_C \left(1\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the endpoint parametrization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(t)&=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\

Write $P(x,y)=1$ and $Q(x,y)=x y$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=-1, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(2 - t\right)\cdot \left(- 2 t\right)\cdot \left(-2\right) \\
&=- 4 t^{2} + 8 t.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\

&=\left[- \frac{4 t^{3}}{3} + 4 t^{2} - t\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=- \frac{4 t^{3}}{3} + 4 t^{2} - t, \\
F(1)&=- \frac{4 \left(1\right)^{3}}{3} + 4 \left(1\right)^{2} - \left(1\right) \\

F(0)&=- \frac{4 \left(0\right)^{3}}{3} + 4 \left(0\right)^{2} - \left(0\right) \\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\
&=\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=\frac{5}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments

question.:question/problem:
The path $C$ is the line segment from $A(2,0)$ to $B(1,-2)$, traversed from $A$ to $B$. Evaluate

$$
\int_C \left(y\right)\,\mathrm{d}x+\left(x y\right)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the endpoint parametrization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{r}(t)&=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}) \\
&=\langle 2,0\rangle+t\langle -1,-2\rangle \\
&=\langle 2 - t,- 2 t\rangle,\qquad 0\le t\le1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x(t)=2 - t$, $y(t)=- 2 t$, and $\mathbf{r}'(t)=\langle -1,-2\rangle$. Thus $\mathrm{d}x=-1\,\mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}y=-2\,\mathrm{d}t$.

Write $P(x,y)=y$ and $Q(x,y)=x y$. Evaluate $P$ and $Q$ along the segment and retain their corresponding signed differentials:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P\,x'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(- 2 t\right)\cdot \left(-1\right) \\
&=2 t, \\
Q\,y'(t)&=\left(1\right)\cdot \left(2 - t\right)\cdot \left(- 2 t\right)\cdot \left(-2\right) \\
&=- 4 t^{2} + 8 t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $I$ denote the requested integral. Using the power rule gives an antiderivative $F(t)$ and the endpoint evaluation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(P\,x'(t)+Q\,y'(t)\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\int_{0}^{1}\left(- 4 t^{2} + 10 t\right)\,\mathrm{d}t \\
&=\left[- \frac{4 t^{3}}{3} + 5 t^{2}\right]_{0}^{1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(t)&=- \frac{4 t^{3}}{3} + 5 t^{2}, \\
F(1)&=- \frac{4 \left(1\right)^{3}}{3} + 5 \left(1\right)^{2} \\
&=\frac{11}{3}, \\
F(0)&=- \frac{4 \left(0\right)^{3}}{3} + 5 \left(0\right)^{2} \\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
I&=F(1)-F(0) \\
&=\left(\frac{11}{3}\right)-\left(0\right) \\
&=\frac{11}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$
